name: CagriSema
class: Amylin analog plus GLP-1 agonist combination
evidenceNote: Several large phase 3 randomized trials, including REDEFINE 1 (3,417 adults) and REDEFINE 2 (1,206 adults with type 2 diabetes), have been published. It is under FDA review but not yet approved.
summary: CagriSema pairs the amylin analog cagrilintide with semaglutide in one weekly shot. It cut weight about 20% in phase 3 and is under FDA review.
keyTakeaway: CagriSema is Novo Nordisk's weekly injection combining cagrilintide, a long-acting copy of the satiety hormone amylin, with semaglutide, the GLP-1 drug in Wegovy. In the 68-week REDEFINE 1 trial, adults without diabetes lost 20.4% of body weight against 3.0% on placebo. In a head-to-head trial it fell short of matching tirzepatide. Novo filed with the FDA in December 2025 and expects a decision in late 2026. It is not approved, and anything sold online under the name is not the real drug.

blocks.text: CagriSema is a fixed-dose combination of two peptides given together once a week: cagrilintide 2.4 mg and semaglutide 2.4 mg. Semaglutide is the GLP-1 receptor agonist already sold as Wegovy and Ozempic. Cagrilintide is a long-acting analog of amylin, a hormone the pancreas releases alongside insulin after a meal [1][3].

Novo Nordisk developed the pairing to test whether two satiety signals produce more weight loss than one. It is being studied for weight management in adults with obesity or overweight with related conditions, and separately in type 2 diabetes [4][6].

Amylin helps signal fullness after eating. In a 26-week phase 2 trial of 706 adults, cagrilintide alone produced weight loss of 6.0% to 10.8% depending on dose, against 3.0% on placebo, and its top dose edged out liraglutide, an older GLP-1 drug [1]. Nausea, constipation, and diarrhea were the most common side effects [1].

Semaglutide works on a different receptor. It mimics GLP-1, a gut hormone released after meals that raises insulin when blood sugar is high and dampens appetite. At 2.4 mg a week, semaglutide alone already has established weight-loss and cardiovascular benefits [3].

Because amylin and GLP-1 act through separate receptors, the idea is that their effects add up. Novo describes the combination as showing that cagrilintide adds weight loss beyond what GLP-1 biology achieves alone [5]. REDEFINE 1 included small single-drug arms to test that, alongside its main comparison with placebo [3].

No, not as of November 2026. Novo Nordisk submitted a new drug application to the FDA for CagriSema 2.4 mg/2.4 mg in adults with overweight or obesity, based on the REDEFINE 1 and REDEFINE 2 trials, which together enrolled more than 4,600 adults [2].

In its report for the first nine months of 2026, Novo listed a US decision as expected in the fourth quarter of 2026 and said it is preparing a US launch in early 2027, subject to approval [6]. Novo has also filed in China, where it expects a decision in the first half of 2028 [6].

blocks.text: REDEFINE 1 randomized 3,417 adults without diabetes who had a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with a weight-related condition. Over 68 weeks, on top of lifestyle advice, the combination group lost an average of 20.4% of body weight compared with 3.0% on placebo, a difference of 17.3 percentage points. More people on CagriSema reached each threshold the trial tracked, up to 30% weight loss [3].

REDEFINE 2 tested the same doses in 1,206 adults with type 2 diabetes. Weight fell 13.7% against 3.4% on placebo over 68 weeks, and 73.5% reached a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c, a three-month blood sugar average) of 6.5% or less, compared with 15.9% on placebo [4]. Weight loss was smaller than in the trial of people without diabetes.

blocks.text: The head-to-head comparison was a setback. In REDEFINE 4, 809 adults received CagriSema or tirzepatide 15 mg for 84 weeks with everyone aware of their assignment. If everyone stayed on treatment, weight loss was 23.0% with CagriSema and 25.5% with tirzepatide; counting everyone regardless of adherence, it was 20.2% and 23.6%. The trial failed to show CagriSema was no worse than tirzepatide [5].

Side effects are mainly digestive. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, or abdominal pain affected 79.6% of people on CagriSema in REDEFINE 1 versus 39.9% on placebo, and 72.5% versus 34.4% in REDEFINE 2. Most episodes were mild to moderate and faded over time [3][4]. Longer and higher-dose trials are still running [6].

Because the product is not approved, no pharmacy can legally dispense genuine CagriSema in the United States. Vials marketed online as cagrilintide, or as cagrilintide blended with semaglutide, are research chemicals of unknown content and purity. The trial results above apply only to Novo Nordisk's product given at the studied doses under medical supervision [3].
